The plunger of syringe 1 moves in noticeably and springs back when released. The plunger of syringe 2 hardly moves at all.

items.q: What is the density of sample B in SI units? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: 8.96 is the density in g/cm³. Convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Value: you divided volume by mass. Density is mass per volume, ρ = m/V.

items.q: Which two samples could be made of the same metal?
options: A and C
A and B
B and D
C and D

items.q: Sample C is cut into two pieces, one twice the volume of the other. How does the density of the smaller piece compare with the density of sample C?
options: It is the same
It is one third as large
It is half as large
It is two thirds as large

items.q: A block of the same metal as sample D has a volume of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. What is its mass? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used 19.3 g/cm³ with a volume in m³. Convert the density first: 19.3 g/cm³ = 1.93 × 10⁴ kg/m³.
Value: you divided the volume by the density. m = ρV.

items.q: What does the experiment show about the two fluids?
options: Water is nearly incompressible; air is easily compressed
Both fluids are incompressible, since neither leaks out
The air is nearly incompressible, but the water is compressed
Neither is a fluid, because they are trapped in the syringe

items.q: What happens to the density of the air in syringe 1 while the plunger is pushed in?
options: It increases, because the same mass occupies a smaller volume
It stays the same, because no air leaves the syringe
It decreases, because the particles are pushed apart
It stays the same, because density is a property of the material

items.q: When a fluid is treated as ideal on the exam, which property is it assumed to have?
options: Its density stays the same as it flows and is squeezed
The fluid sticks to the walls of its container
The fluid has no mass, so it exerts no forces
The fluid keeps its shape when it is poured

items.q: Why is liquid water much harder to compress than air?
options: Water particles already touch; air particles are far apart
Water particles are locked in fixed places, as in a solid
Water has a larger mass than air, so it is harder to move
Air particles attract each other more strongly than water particles do

items.q: Which of these is a fluid?
options: Honey
A steel ball bearing
A block of ice
A rubber band

items.q: A rectangular swimming pool is 10.0 m long, 5.0 m wide and filled to a depth of 2.0 m with water of density 1000 kg/m³. What is the mass of the water? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the weight in newtons (you multiplied by g). The question asks for the mass, m = ρV.
Value: you added the dimensions. Volume is length × width × depth.

items.q: Cube X is made of the same material as cube Y but has sides twice as long. How does the mass of X compare with the mass of Y?
options: 8 times as large
2 times as large
4 times as large
The same

items.q: A sealed bottle of air is warmed in the sun, and its volume does not change. What happens to the density of the air inside?
options: It stays the same, because m and V do not change
It increases, because the particles move faster
It decreases, because warm air is less dense
It increases, because the pressure inside rises

items.q: A 250 cm³ sample of olive oil has a mass of 0.229 kg. What is its density in SI units? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the volume in cm³ with a mass in kg. Convert: 250 cm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Value: 250 cm³ is 0.250 L, not 0.250 m³. 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, so 250 cm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

items.q: A brick is weighed, then sawn into two halves. Predict how each quantity for one half compares with the whole brick.
What makes a liquid different from a solid at the level of its particles?
options: The particles can slide past one another, so it flows
The particles are much farther apart, so the liquid is easy to compress
The particles do not attract each other
The particles stop moving when the liquid is at rest

items.q: How does the pressure at J compare with the pressure at K?
options: It is the same, because J and K are at the same depth
It is larger at J, because J is nearer the wall
It is larger at K, because more water is above K
It is smaller at J, because the water at J pushes sideways

items.q: What is the absolute pressure at L? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the gauge pressure, ρgh. Absolute pressure adds the air pressing on the surface: P = P₀ + ρgh.
Value: you used the depth of J and K (1.5 m). L is 4.5 m below the surface.

items.q: What is the gauge pressure at L? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the absolute pressure. Gauge pressure is the pressure above atmospheric: P_gauge = ρgh.
Value: you left out g. P_gauge = ρgh.

items.q: L is 3 times as deep as J. How does the absolute pressure at L compare with that at J?
options: Larger, but less than 3 times as large
Exactly 3 times as large
Exactly 9 times as large
The same, because the water is incompressible

items.q: Why does the graph not pass through zero at zero depth?
options: It reads absolute pressure, which includes the air's push
The sensor is faulty, because there is no water above it at the surface
Water pressure is largest at the surface and decreases with depth
The sensor reads gauge pressure, which includes the weight of the diver

items.q: Use the slope of the graph to find the density of the lake water. Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you kept the slope in kPa/m. Convert to Pa/m (× 1000) before dividing by g.
Value: you divided the total reading by the depth, which includes the 101 kPa from the air. Use the slope: the change in pressure over the change in depth.

items.q: The diver repeats the measurements in seawater, which is denser than lake water. How would the new graph differ?
options: Same intercept, steeper slope
Higher intercept, same slope
Same intercept, same slope
Higher intercept, steeper slope

items.q: Which statement explains why pressure increases with depth in the lake?
options: Deeper water holds up the weight of more water above it
Water is compressed at depth, so it becomes much denser
The pressure force at each depth points down, so it adds up
Deeper water is colder, so its particles move faster

items.q: A woman of weight 600 N stands on one heel of area 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m². What pressure does the heel exert on the floor? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied force by area. Pressure is force per area, P = F/A.
Value: you divided area by force. P = F/A.

items.q: A student says, "Pressure is a force, so it has a direction." What is the best correction?
options: Pressure is force per area, a scalar; its force on a surface is perpendicular to it
Pressure is a force, but its direction is straight down, toward Earth
Pressure has a direction: in a fluid it points toward the bottom of the container
Pressure is the same as weight, so it points down and is measured in newtons

items.q: Three containers have different shapes: a tall narrow tube, a wide bowl and a cone that widens upward. All are filled with water to the same height. Where is the pressure at the bottom greatest?
options: It is the same in all three
In the wide bowl, because it holds the most water
In the narrow tube, because the water is concentrated
In the cone, because its walls push the water down

items.q: A tire gauge reads 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa. Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. What is the absolute pressure of the air inside the tire? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the gauge reading. A tire gauge reads pressure above atmospheric, so add P₀ to get absolute pressure.
Value: you subtracted P₀. Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.

items.q: How deep in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) is the absolute pressure 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa? Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you set ρgh equal to the whole 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The air already provides 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa; the water adds only the other 0.5 × 10⁵ Pa.

items.q: A sealed submarine window is 20 m below the surface of the sea. Predict how the gauge pressure on the window changes for each separate change.

variables.name: The window is made twice as large, at 20 m
The submarine moves to fresh water, at 20 m

items.q: A water tower supplies a house. Why are water towers built tall?
options: A greater height of water gives a greater pressure at the taps below
A taller tower holds more water, which flows out more quickly
Water high up has less pressure, so it is pulled down to the house
A tall tower keeps the water away from the air, which lowers its pressure

items.q: What is the buoyant force on the cylinder when it is fully under water? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the scale reading, the tension in the scale. The buoyant force is the drop in the reading: weight in air minus reading in water.
Value: that is the cylinder's weight. The buoyant force is the part of the weight the water now supports: 2.65 N − 1.67 N.

items.q: Why does the scale reading stop changing once the depth is more than 10 cm?
options: The cylinder is fully submerged, so the volume of water it displaces stops growing
The water pressure stops increasing below 10 cm of depth
The cylinder's weight decreases until it matches the buoyant force
The buoyant force reaches its largest possible value for any object in water

items.q: Use the data to find the density of the cylinder's metal. Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the reading in water in place of the weight. ρ_object/ρ_water = weight / buoyant force when fully submerged: 2.65 N / 0.98 N.
Value: you divided the buoyant force by the weight; the ratio is upside down. The object is denser than water, so its density must be above 1000 kg/m³.

items.q: The experiment is repeated in salt water, which is denser than fresh water. Compared with the fresh-water value, what is the scale reading when the cylinder is fully submerged?
options: Smaller, because the buoyant force is larger
Larger, because salt water pushes down harder on the top
The same, because the cylinder displaces the same volume
Larger, because the cylinder's weight increases in salt water

items.q: While the cylinder hangs at rest fully under water, which equation describes the forces on it?
options: F_T + F_b = F_g
F_T = F_g + F_b
F_b = F_g
F_T = F_g

items.q: Rank the buoyant forces on the three blocks, from largest to smallest.
options: Z, then Y, then X
X, then Y, then Z
X, Y and Z are equal
Y, then X, then Z

items.q: What is the density of block X? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down. A floating block is less dense than water; ρ_X = ρ_water × (fraction submerged) = 1000 × ½.

items.q: How does the buoyant force on block Y compare with the gravitational force on Y?
options: They are equal, because Y is floating at rest
The buoyant force is larger, because Y floats
The buoyant force is smaller, because Y is partly above the water
The buoyant force is larger, because Y is denser than X

items.q: Block Z rests on the bottom. Which statement about the forces on Z is correct?
options: F_b is less than Z's weight; the floor's normal force makes up the rest
There is no buoyant force on Z, because water is not pushing up from under it
The buoyant force equals Z's weight, because Z is at rest
The buoyant force on Z is smaller than on X, because Z is denser

items.q: Block X is pushed down until it is just fully under water and held there. How does the buoyant force on it now compare with before?
options: Twice as large
The same
Half as large
Four times as large

items.q: A rock of volume 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is fully under water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). What is the buoyant force on it? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the mass of the displaced water in kg. The buoyant force is its weight: multiply by g.

items.q: A lead block and an aluminum block have the same volume and are both held fully under water. A student claims the lead block feels the larger buoyant force because it is heavier. What is the best response?
options: The forces are equal: each displaces the same volume of water
The claim is right: a heavier object pushes more water aside
The aluminum feels more, because it is less dense and tends to rise
The lead feels more, because it sinks deeper and feels more pressure

items.q: An ice cube (ρ = 917 kg/m³) floats in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). What fraction of its volume is below the surface? Give a decimal.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down; a fraction below the surface must be less than 1. V_sub/V = ρ_ice/ρ_water.
Value: that is the fraction above the surface. The fraction below is ρ_ice/ρ_water.

items.q: A 0.60 kg wooden block floats at rest in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). What volume of water does it displace? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you set the volume equal to weight/density. Floating: ρ_w V g = m g, so g cancels and V = m/ρ_w.
Value: you used a density for wood. The displaced volume follows from the water's density: V = m/ρ_water.

items.q: A steel ball (ρ = 7800 kg/m³) is released from rest under water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). Neglecting the water's drag, what is the size of its acceleration just after release? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that ignores the buoyant force. Newton's second law: ma = mg − F_b, with F_b = ρ_w V g.
Value: that is F_b/m alone. The net force is the weight minus the buoyant force: a = g(1 − ρ_w/ρ_steel).

items.q: A floating barge is loaded with extra cargo and still floats. Predict how each quantity compares with before the cargo was added.

variables.name: Volume of water the barge displaces

items.q: Imagine a parcel of water, the same shape as a submerged stone, sitting at rest inside a lake. Why does this show that the buoyant force on the stone equals the weight of the water it displaces?
options: The parcel is at rest, so the water around it holds up its weight; the stone gets the same push
The parcel has no weight in water, so the stone has no weight either
Water pressure is equal at each depth in the lake, so objects feel equal forces
The parcel sinks at the same rate as the stone, so the forces on them match

items.q: What is the volume flow rate of the water? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided area by speed. Volume flow rate is area × speed, Av.

items.q: What is the speed of the water at section 2? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down. The water must speed up where the pipe is narrower: v₂ = v₁A₁/A₂.
Value: the speed changes. The same volume each second must pass through a smaller area: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

items.q: What is the absolute pressure at section 2? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the sign is reversed. Where the water moves faster, its pressure is lower: P₂ = P₁ + ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²).
Value: you left out the ½ in the kinetic term. Bernoulli uses ½ρv².
Value: you used ½ρ(Δv)². Use the difference of the squares: ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²).

items.q: A student predicts that the pressure is higher at section 2 because the water is squeezed into a narrower pipe. Which response is correct?
options: The pressure is lower at section 2, because the water speeds up and is pushed from behind
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the narrow walls push in on the water
The pressure is the same at both sections, because the water is incompressible
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the same flow rate passes through less area

items.q: Which principle sets the speed at section 2, and which sets the pressure there?
options: Continuity sets the speed; Bernoulli then sets the pressure
Bernoulli sets the speed; continuity then sets the pressure
Bernoulli alone sets both, with no need for continuity
Continuity alone sets both, because the pipe is horizontal

items.q: What is the speed of the water as it leaves the hole? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is v². Take the square root: v = √(2gh).
Value: you lost the factor of 2. ρgh = ½ρv² gives v = √(2gh).

items.q: Why can the speed of the water surface in the tank be taken as zero?
options: By continuity, the wide surface moves far more slowly than the water in the small hole
The water at the surface is at atmospheric pressure, so it does not move
The surface is the highest point, so its kinetic energy is converted to potential energy
The water in the tank is at rest; just the jet moves

items.q: A second hole is made 7.2 m below the surface of a taller tank of the same kind. How does the jet speed from this hole compare with the 1.8 m hole?
options: Twice as fast
Four times as fast
√2 times as fast
The same

items.q: The hole is replaced by one with half the area, at the same depth. What happens to the jet's speed and to the volume flow rate out of the hole?
options: Speed unchanged; flow rate halved
Speed doubled; flow rate unchanged
Speed halved; flow rate halved
Speed doubled; flow rate doubled

items.q: The hole has an area of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². What is the volume flow rate out of it? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used v² in place of v. Find v = √(2gh) first, then multiply by the area.

items.q: You put your thumb over part of the end of a garden hose, and the water sprays out faster. Why?
options: The same volume per second leaves through a smaller area
Your thumb adds energy to the water as it squeezes past
The pressure in the jet rises under your thumb, which pushes the water out faster
Water is compressed under your thumb and expands as it leaves

items.q: Treat blood as an ideal fluid. It flows at 0.30 m/s in an artery. At a narrowed section, the area is one third of the normal area. What is the blood's speed in the narrowed section? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the speed goes up where the area goes down. v₂ = v₁(A₁/A₂) = 3 × 0.30 m/s.

items.q: Water flows at a steady speed up a vertical pipe of constant cross section. What is the difference in pressure between two points 5.0 m apart in height? Use g = 9.8 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out g. The pressure difference is ρgΔy.
Value: there is no ½ here. With equal speeds the kinetic terms cancel, leaving P₁ − P₂ = ρg(y₂ − y₁).

items.q: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of which conservation law, applied to a moving fluid?
options: Conservation of energy
Conservation of mass
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of angular momentum

items.q: Water flows through a full horizontal pipe that widens to twice its diameter. Predict how each quantity in the wide part compares with the narrow part.
A smooth stream of water falling from a faucet gets narrower as it falls. Which explanation is correct?
options: It speeds up as it falls, so by continuity its area shrinks
Air pressure squeezes the stream more and more as it falls
The water is compressed by its own weight as it falls
Some water evaporates from the stream, so less is left
